chapter.name: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Parliament.
(I) It comprises only those representatives who have been directly elected by the people.
(II) It controls and guides the work of the government.
(III) The old Parliament building, built in the 1920s, hosted the deliberations of the Constituent Assembly.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar said in 1949 that the Constitution 'is not a mere lawyer's document; it is a vehicle of life'. Using the Introduction, give three points that show how it carries life into the people's governance.
questions.a: It laid foundational principles for the whole nation, such as Universal Adult Franchise, so it shapes the life of every adult citizen who can vote. It also set up a system in which the people's votes elect the Lok Sabha and a majority group among them forms the government, so it carries ordinary citizens' decisions into governance.
s: Says it laid foundational principles for the nation
Links it to the right of every adult citizen to vote
Links it to the people's votes producing a government

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A majority group from among the elected representatives of the Lok Sabha forms the government.
Reason (R): Members of the Lok Sabha are elected by an electoral college of the states.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Meena, a Class 8 student in Pune, says: 'The government is chosen by the President, so my vote has nothing to do with it.' Which chain from the chapter best answers her?
questions.a: The people directly elect Lok Sabha members, and a majority group among them forms the government
o: The people directly elect Lok Sabha members, and a majority group among them forms the government
The people directly elect the President, who then forms the government from the members of the Rajya Sabha
The Constituent Assembly chose the first government, and later governments continue on its consent
Members of the Rajya Sabha are chosen by the people, and a majority group of them forms the government

questions.q: The Introduction says the citizens of a free country 'could now make decisions about their own governance'. (a) Which document did the chapter say they drafted first? (b) Explain how the principle that document laid down, Universal Adult Franchise, links an ordinary adult to who forms the government.
questions.a: (a) The Constitution of independent India. (b) Universal Adult Franchise lets every adult citizen vote; the people directly elect the Lok Sabha's members; a majority group from among them forms the government.
s: Names the Constitution
Links the adult's vote to Lok Sabha members and to the majority group forming the government

questions.q: Ravi says: 'The new Parliament building was constructed only to add more seats for members.' Test his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does say it was constructed to accommodate growing needs, including capacity, which is the need of space. But it names other needs too: technology, sustainability and safety. So 'only' is wrong.
s: Gives the verdict: partly right
Accepts capacity as one of the needs
Corrects 'only' by naming technology, sustainability or safety

questions.q: A magazine says: 'There have been 18 Lok Sabhas since 1952, and the 18th was constituted in 2019.' Which part of this does the chapter correct?
questions.a: The 18th Lok Sabha was constituted in June 2024, not in 2019
o: The 18th Lok Sabha was constituted in June 2024, not in 2019
The first Lok Sabha was constituted in 1957 rather than in 1952
The count of Lok Sabhas should start from the 18th, not from the first
The 18th Lok Sabha was constituted before the 17th was formed

questions.q: An imagined country lets an adult citizen vote only if she owns land worth more than Rs 5 lakh (illustrative). Which part of the chapter's description of Universal Adult Franchise does this rule go against?
questions.a: The right to vote irrespective of social or economic background
o: The right to vote irrespective of social or economic background
The right to vote irrespective of gender
The right to vote irrespective of race
The right to vote irrespective of religion

questions.q:
Three imagined countries (illustrative) each say their government rests on the people's consent. Country X: all adults vote for a House directly, but the head of government is named by a hereditary ruler, not by a majority of the House. Country Y: men over 18 vote for a House directly and a majority group of it forms the government, and women may not vote. Country Z: all adult citizens, whatever their gender, race, religion or background, vote directly for the House and a majority group of it forms the government.
(a) Which link of the chapter's chain fails in X?
(b) Which fails in Y?
(c) Which country can the chapter's reasoning call a government functioning with the people's consent?
(d) Name the three links of that chain in order.
questions.a: (a) The link that a majority group from among the elected representatives forms the government. (b) Universal Adult Franchise, the right of all adult citizens to vote irrespective of gender, since women may not vote. (c) Country Z. (d) Every adult citizen has the right to vote; the people directly elect representatives who become Lok Sabha members; a majority group from among them forms the government.
s: Identifies the failing link in X
Identifies the failing link in Y
Names Country Z
Names the first two links of the chain
Names the third link in order

questions.q: A school group is planning a visit. (a) Which building should they visit to see where the Constituent Assembly held its deliberations, and what is it called now? (b) Which building houses today's Parliament, and name two of the needs the chapter lists for it?
questions.a: (a) The old Parliament building, now called Samvidhan Sadan, built in the 1920s. (b) The new Parliament building, Sansad Bhavan, built for growing needs including capacity, technology, sustainability and safety; any two earn the mark.
s: Names Samvidhan Sadan as the old building where the Assembly met
Names Sansad Bhavan and two of the needs the chapter lists

questions.q: Differentiate between 'the Parliament' and 'the government' as the Introduction uses them.
questions.a: The Parliament is the supreme legislative body: it makes laws, comprises all elected and nominated representatives, and controls and guides the work of the government. The government is formed by a majority group from among the elected representatives of the Lok Sabha.
s: Describes the Parliament as the law-making body that comprises all elected and nominated representatives and controls and guides the government
Describes the government as formed by a majority group from among the elected Lok Sabha representatives

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with what it means in the chapter, given in Column B.
Column A: 1. Universal Adult Franchise  2. Lok Sabha  3. Parliament  4. The government
Column B: a. formed by a majority group from among the elected representatives  b. every adult citizen may vote whatever her gender or religion  c. the House whose members the people choose by direct election  d. the body of all elected and nominated representatives that controls and guides the government

The Introduction calls the Parliament 'the supreme legislative body'. A student says: 'Supreme means the Parliament can do anything, so it is the same as the government.' (a) What does the chapter put in brackets to explain 'legislative'? (b) Using the chapter, give one reason why the Parliament and the government are not the same.
questions.a: (a) That it makes laws for the country. (b) The government is formed by a majority group from among the elected representatives of the Lok Sabha, while the Parliament comprises all elected and nominated representatives and controls and guides the work of the government.
s: States that legislative means it makes laws for the country
Gives a reason from the chapter that separates Parliament from government

questions.q: (a) Name two of the carvings that decorate the walls of the new building. (b) One student remarks that the building 'houses so many ancient symbols'. Which other remark in the students' conversation tells us why old symbols belong in a new building?
questions.a: (a) Any two of peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns, freedom fighters. (b) 'Democracy must look ahead, but never forget its roots.'
s: Names two carvings
Gives the look-ahead-but-roots remark

questions.q: At a school debate, a speaker says: 'The old Parliament building served for over seven decades, so a new one was unnecessary.' Which point from the chapter answers her most directly?
questions.a: The new building was built for growing needs such as capacity, technology and safety
o: The new building was built for growing needs such as capacity, technology and safety
The Constituent Assembly's deliberations took place in the old building, now called Samvidhan Sadan
The old building was constructed in the 1920s and is now called Samvidhan Sadan, as the Assembly's home
The new building has a three-sided design, not a square or round one, reflecting balance and purpose

questions.q: A student counts Lok Sabhas for a chart, starting with the first, which the chapter says was constituted in the year ___.

Students of a school in Madurai draft four lines for a wall chart called 'Our Parliament'.
Line 1: 'Universal Adult Franchise guarantees all adult citizens the right to vote irrespective of social or economic background, gender, race or religion.'
Line 2: 'The Parliament comprises only elected representatives and has no say in the work of the government.'
Line 3: 'Samvidhan Sadan is the name of the new building, built for growing needs of capacity and safety; the Constituent Assembly met in it.'
Line 4: 'The first Lok Sabha was in 1952 and the 18th was constituted in June 2024.'
(a) Which two lines can stay as they are?
(b) Rewrite Line 2 correctly.
(c) Rewrite Line 3 correctly.
(d) A visitor reads the uncorrected Line 2. What would she wrongly conclude about the Parliament's relation to the government, and what is the correct relation?
questions.a: (a) Lines 1 and 4. (b) The Parliament comprises all elected and nominated representatives of the people and controls and guides the work of the government. (c) Samvidhan Sadan is the old building, constructed in the 1920s, where the Constituent Assembly met; the new building, Sansad Bhavan, was built for growing needs. (d) She would conclude that the Parliament has no say over the government's work; in fact it controls and guides it.
s: Picks Lines 1 and 4 as correct
Corrects Line 2: elected and nominated, and controls and guides the government
Corrects Line 3: Samvidhan Sadan is the old building, Sansad Bhavan the new one
Says the visitor would think the Parliament has no say, and gives the correct relation: it controls and guides the government

questions.q:
A committee is choosing between two designs for a hall in the new building (illustrative). Design A: green construction, which the chapter says cuts electricity use by a stated percentage, costs an extra Rs 12 lakh. Design B: a partial measure, costs an extra Rs 5 lakh and saves half as much as Design A. The hall would otherwise use 2,40,000 units a year at Rs 8 a unit, and will be used for 40 years.
(a) What percentage cut does the chapter give for green construction?
(b) How many rupees a year does Design A save?
(c) Over 40 years, what is each option's saving less its extra cost?
(d) Which design should the committee choose on electricity savings alone?
s: States 30 per cent
Computes Rs 5,76,000 a year
Computes the net saving of each option over 40 years
Chooses Design A with the difference of Rs 1,08,20,000

questions.q: A Class 6 student asks five questions about Parliament. Answer each from the chapter and then say what the answers show about the difference between the Parliament and the government. (a) Who makes laws for the country? (b) Who forms the government? (c) Who controls and guides the work of the government? (d) Who sit in the Parliament, by the chapter's words? (e) Give one sentence on the difference.
questions.a: (a) The Parliament, the supreme legislative body. (b) A majority group from among the elected representatives of the Lok Sabha. (c) The Parliament. (d) All elected and nominated representatives of the people. (e) The government is formed from a majority group of the Lok Sabha's elected representatives, while the Parliament, which includes all elected and nominated representatives, makes the laws and controls and guides the government's work.
s: Says the Parliament makes laws
Says a majority group of Lok Sabha representatives forms the government
Says the Parliament controls and guides the government
Says elected and nominated representatives sit in the Parliament
Gives a correct one-line difference

questions.q: A student's closing remark on the visit is: 'Democracy must look ahead, but never forget its roots.' Write two observations from a visit to the new building that could lead to this remark, one looking ahead and one about roots, and say which feature of the building holds both.
questions.a: Looking ahead: the building uses green construction that cuts electricity use by 30 per cent and was built for growing needs of capacity, technology, sustainability and safety. Roots: the walls are carved with peacocks, lotuses, tribal art, temple patterns and freedom fighters. One building holds both, a new structure carrying old symbols such as the Ashokan emblem.
s: Gives an observation about looking ahead
Gives an observation about roots
Names the new building carrying ancient symbols as holding both

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution makers gave India a second House, the Rajya Sabha, in addition to the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): It was felt that a single directly elected House would be inadequate to meet the challenges independent India would face.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Define federalism as the chapter does.
(b) A state official says, 'One directly elected House is enough for a country.' Give the chapter's reason for not accepting this.
questions.a: (a) A form of government where power is distributed between the centre, the states and local governments. (b) It was felt that a single directly elected House would be inadequate to meet the challenges independent India would face, so a Council of States was needed in the spirit of federalism.
s: Defines federalism as power shared between centre, states and local governments
Gives the inadequacy of a single directly elected House as the reason for a Council of States

questions.q: True or False? 'The Indian Parliament consists of two parts only, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Indian Parliament is composed of the President and two houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
s: Gives the verdict: false
Corrects it: the President together with the two houses compose the Parliament

questions.q: Differentiate between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the way their members are chosen, and give one example of a name by which each is known.
questions.a: Lok Sabha members are chosen by direct election based on universal adult suffrage; it is also called the House of the People or the Lower House. Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by an electoral college; it is also called the Council of States or the Upper House.
s: Contrasts direct election with indirect election by an electoral college
Gives one correct alternative name for each House

questions.q:
Class 8 runs a model Parliament in a school (illustrative). Chamber P has 40 members directly elected by all students; Chamber Q has 10 members elected by the class representatives. The Principal signs off every decision, as the head of the model. Every bill passes through both chambers and takes 3 hours in each; 12 bills are planned this term. The school head proposes to drop Chamber Q to save time. The class's stated aim is to model India's Parliament faithfully.
(a) Which chamber matches the Lok Sabha and which the Rajya Sabha?
(b) Which part of India's Parliament does the Principal's role match?
(c) How many hours would dropping Chamber Q save this term?
(d) What does the chapter say was felt about a single directly elected House, and should the class drop Chamber Q given its stated aim?
questions.a: (a) P matches the Lok Sabha, Q the Rajya Sabha. (b) The President, who is part of the Parliament along with the two houses. (c) Each bill takes 3 hours in each of two chambers: 12 x 3 x 2 = 72 hours; with one chamber 36 hours; so 36 hours are saved. (d) The chapter says a single directly elected House would be inadequate to meet the challenges, and a Council of States with a different composition and election was needed in the spirit of federalism. Since the aim is to model India's Parliament faithfully, the class should keep Chamber Q: the 36 hours saved do not serve that aim.
s: Matches P to the Lok Sabha and Q to the Rajya Sabha
Names the President
Computes 36 hours saved
States the chapter's view and decides to keep Q given the aim

questions.q: A school chart has a column headed 'Common to both Houses'. Which line from the chapter belongs there?
questions.a: For each state, seats in both Houses are based on the state's population
o: For each state, seats in both Houses are based on the state's population
Their members are chosen by direct election based on universal adult suffrage in every state
A maximum of 550 members is envisaged by the Constitution for each of them
Both are presided over by the Vice President of India as chairperson of the House

questions.q: Compare the two Houses to find what the chapter says was designed to be different. (a) Give the two names of each House. (b) Say how members of each are chosen. (c) Say who presides over each. (d) State one thing the two have in common about states. (e) Which of the differences in (b) and (c) does the chapter itself say was deliberately designed to be different, and why does that matter for federalism?
questions.a: (a) Lok Sabha: House of the People, Lower House; Rajya Sabha: Council of States, Upper House. (b) Lok Sabha: direct election based on universal adult suffrage; Rajya Sabha: indirect election by an electoral college. (c) Lok Sabha: a Speaker elected by its members; Rajya Sabha: the Vice President of India as chairperson. (d) In both, the share of each state is based on its population. (e) The composition and process of election of the Rajya Sabha; this matters because the Council of States was felt to be needed in the spirit of federalism, and a differently chosen House can represent a different balance of national unity and local interests.
s: Gives correct names for both Houses
Contrasts direct and indirect election
Names the Speaker and the Vice President as presiding officers
States that seats in both depend on each state's population
Identifies composition and election process, with the link to federalism

questions.q:
An imagined House has candidates for new interpretation languages (illustrative). Interpretation costs a flat Rs 4 lakh a language a year, and the budget allows only three new languages this year. MPs who would use each: Santhali 20, Konkani 12, Kashmiri 9, Tulu 4, Sindhi 2 (47 in all). Plan P adds Santhali, Konkani and Kashmiri; Plan Q adds Konkani, Tulu and Sindhi because their interpreters are nearer. The chapter's aim for interpretation is to make Parliamentary discussions accessible to all.
(a) After the chapter's six additions to its 12 languages, how many languages are covered now?
(b) What is the yearly cost of covering them at Rs 4 lakh each?
(c) How many MPs does each plan reach?
(d) Which plan should the House adopt, and by how many MPs do they differ?
questions.a: (a) 12 + 6 = 18. (b) 18 x 4 = Rs 72 lakh. (c) Plan P: 20 + 12 + 9 = 41 MPs; Plan Q: 12 + 4 + 2 = 18 MPs. (d) Plan P, since both cost the same and it makes discussions accessible to 23 more MPs (41 - 18).
s: Computes 18
Computes Rs 72 lakh
Computes 41 and 18
Chooses Plan P with the difference of 23 MPs

questions.q: A country keeps all its legislative and executive power in one capital, with no say for its provinces or local bodies. Judged by the chapter's definition, what is missing from this country?
questions.a: Federalism, power distributed between the centre, the states and local governments
o: Federalism, power distributed between the centre, the states and local governments
A bicameral legislature, with the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha as its two Houses of Parliament
Universal adult suffrage, which is how the members of the Lok Sabha are elected
A Speaker, who ensures that the rules of debate are followed in the House

questions.q: Rahul says: 'Britain's system inspired India's parliamentary democracy, yet our Constitution makers also had the memory of the mahajanapadas and of village panchayats.' Test his statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter says Britain's system inspired the system of parliamentary democracy. It also names, among the experiences of freedom fighters and Constitution makers, the memory of the ancient republics (mahajanapadas) and the village panchayats where elders made collective decisions.
s: Gives the verdict: right
Confirms Britain's system as the inspiration
Confirms the mahajanapadas and village panchayats as named experiences

questions.q: The chapter says freedom fighters and Constitution makers had 'practical experience gained through participation in British colonial governance structures, even if in a very limited way'. Explain what this experience gave them, and why the chapter adds the phrase about it being limited.
questions.a: It provided familiarity with Parliamentary procedures. The phrase 'even if in a very limited way' tells the reader that their participation in colonial structures was small, so the experience was a help but not the whole root; the chapter names other roots such as the mahajanapadas and village panchayats.
s: States that it gave familiarity with Parliamentary procedures
Notes that the chapter says the participation was 'very limited', so the experience was only one root
Links this to the other roots the chapter names

questions.q: (a) On what occasion, and to whom, was the Sengol handed over in 1947? (b) Where is it placed now, and what was it a reminder of when handed to new rulers, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) It was symbolically handed to Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 14 August 1947, on the occasion of Indian Independence, to mark the transfer of power. (b) It is placed near the Speaker's chair in the new Lok Sabha; it was a reminder that power must be guided by dharma and righteousness.
s: States 14 August 1947 and Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru, marking the transfer of power
States its place near the Speaker's chair and the reminder about dharma and righteousness

questions.q: The makers of the Constitution debated whether India should have a bicameral system. (a) What did they feel about a single directly elected House? (b) Which House did they feel was needed in the spirit of federalism? (c) What was designed to be different about it? (d) What does federalism balance? (e) Give a one-line verdict on why the Lok Sabha alone could not do this.
questions.a: (a) That it would be inadequate to meet the challenges independent India would face. (b) A Council of States, the Rajya Sabha. (c) Its composition and its process of election. (d) National unity and local interests. (e) The Lok Sabha is the directly elected House; the chapter says a Council of States with a different composition and process of election was felt to be needed in the spirit of federalism, so the Lok Sabha alone was not enough.
s: States the inadequacy of a single directly elected House
Names the Council of States as needed in the spirit of federalism
Says composition and election process were designed differently
Says federalism balances national unity and local interests
Gives a reasoned verdict on why one House alone could not do this

questions.q: A speaker at a school debate says: 'The Speaker keeps order in both Houses of Parliament.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The Speaker is elected by Lok Sabha members and orders that House; the Vice President presides over the Rajya Sabha
o: The Speaker is elected by Lok Sabha members and orders that House; the Vice President presides over the Rajya Sabha
The Speaker keeps order in the Lok Sabha, and the President of India keeps order in the Rajya Sabha as its chairperson
The Speaker keeps order in the Rajya Sabha, and the Vice President of India keeps order in the Lok Sabha as its chairperson
Neither House has a presiding officer, because the Prime Minister keeps order in both Houses at once

questions.q:
(a) In which House does a Speaker preside, and who chooses the Speaker?
(b) Why does each House need a presiding officer, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) The Lok Sabha; its members elect the Speaker. (b) To ensure that debates and discussions are conducted in an orderly manner, by conducting sessions, allowing members to speak, maintaining discipline and ensuring that rules are followed.
s: Names the Lok Sabha and election by its members
Gives the purpose: orderly debate, with duties such as discipline and following rules

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Indian Parliament.
(I) The Lok Sabha is also called the House of the People and the Rajya Sabha the Council of States.
(II) The Constitution envisages a maximum of 550 members for the Rajya Sabha.
(III) A structure with two houses is called bicameral.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
III only

questions.q: Show that the Rajya Sabha cannot be the House whose members are all chosen by direct election based on universal adult suffrage.
questions.a: The chapter says the people choose their representatives for the Lok Sabha through direct election based on universal adult suffrage. It says Rajya Sabha MPs are elected indirectly by the electoral college. Direct and indirect election cannot both describe the same House, so the directly elected House is the Lok Sabha.
s: Says the chapter assigns direct election to the Lok Sabha
Says Rajya Sabha MPs are elected indirectly by an electoral college
Concludes that one House cannot be both

questions.q: A neighbouring republic has one legislative chamber whose members are all directly elected. Using the chapter's vocabulary, how does its legislature differ from India's Parliament?
questions.a: It has one house, whereas India's Parliament, being bicameral, has two houses
o: It has one house, whereas India's Parliament, being bicameral, has two houses
It has two houses, whereas India's Parliament, being bicameral, has only one house
It is a federal legislature, whereas India's Parliament is bicameral and is not a federal body
It has a Speaker, whereas India's Parliament has no presiding officer of any kind at all

questions.q: Before six languages (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Manipuri, Urdu and Sanskrit) were added, Parliament offered simultaneous interpretation in ___ languages.
A student writes in a quiz: 'The Lok Sabha will always have exactly 550 members.' What does the chapter say?
questions.a: 550 is the maximum number of members the Constitution envisages for the Lok Sabha
o: 550 is the maximum number of members the Constitution envisages for the Lok Sabha
550 is the fixed number of members of the Rajya Sabha under the Constitution
550 is the number of members the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha have in all
550 is the number of members the Council of Ministers may include in all

questions.q: A guide tells visitors, 'The Union Executive is the Prime Minister alone.' Which statement of the chapter corrects her?
questions.a: The Union Executive consists of the President, the Vice President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
o: The Union Executive consists of the President, the Vice President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
The Union Executive consists of the Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Rajya Sabha, with the Vice President as an adviser
The Union Executive consists of the President and the Prime Minister, with the Vice President as an adviser to both
The Union Executive consists of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, working under the Prime Minister as head

questions.q: Ramesh is an MP of the Rajya Sabha and is made a minister. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: He can be chosen, as ministers come from MPs of both houses, and he is responsible to the Lok Sabha
o: He can be chosen, as ministers come from MPs of both houses, and he is responsible to the Lok Sabha
He cannot be chosen, because ministers are chosen only from the MPs of the Lok Sabha and not the Rajya Sabha
He can be chosen, and as a Rajya Sabha MP he will be collectively responsible to that House alone
He can be chosen, but only after he gives up his seat in the Rajya Sabha

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Parliament's functions.
(I) Amendments to the Constitution are a constitutional function of the Parliament.
(II) The Council of Ministers is chosen only from the MPs of the Lok Sabha.
(III) The executive responsibility of the Parliament means making new laws.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Match each parliamentary activity in Column A with its head in Column B.
Column A: 1. Electing the President and the Vice President  2. Ministers justifying their decisions during the first hour of a session  3. Examining how funds are shared among ministries  4. A bill moving from introduction to presidential assent
Column B: a. Financial accountability  b. Lawmaking  c. Constitutional functions  d. Executive accountability

Assertion (A): The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): The key functions of the Parliament are classified under four heads.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: (a) Name the three components of the Union Executive. (b) A student adds 'the Speaker' to the list. Why is she wrong, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) The President, the Vice President and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. (b) The chapter lists no Speaker in the Union Executive; the Speaker is elected by Lok Sabha members and conducts the House's sessions.
s: Names the three components
Says the Speaker is not in the list, being the Lok Sabha's presiding officer

questions.q: The Parliament frames a law to protect every child's right to free schooling, in line with the Directive Principles of State Policy. Which of the core constitutional values that the chapter says the Parliament must uphold does this serve?
questions.a: Upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies
o: Upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies
Enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage, so that every adult may vote
Following the separation of powers between the legislature, executive and judiciary of the country
Ensuring federalism by distributing power between the centre and the states and local governments

questions.q: Arjun says: 'The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, so the Council answers only to the Prime Minister and to no House.' Test his claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the ministers of the Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister heads the Council, but headship does not remove that responsibility.
s: Gives the verdict: not correct
Says the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha
Explains that heading the Council does not remove that responsibility

questions.q:
Four measures, each described as a law, are before an imagined Parliament (illustrative). Law A gives every adult citizen the right to vote irrespective of gender. Law B says that the Executive may not make laws and the Judiciary may not pass them. Law C gives the states a Council of their own in the legislature. Law D requires the state to provide free schooling in line with the Directive Principles of State Policy. Each law serves one of the four core constitutional values that the chapter says the Parliament must uphold.
(a) Which core value does Law A serve?
(b) Which does Law B serve?
(c) Which does Law C serve?
(d) A member proposes merging Laws B and C into one law to save time. Which two values would then share one law, and does the chapter list them as separate values?
questions.a: (a) Enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage. (b) Following the separation of powers between the legislature, executive and judiciary. (c) Ensuring federalism. (d) Separation of powers and federalism would share one law; the chapter lists them as two separate values.
s: Matches Law A to parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage
Matches Law B to the separation of powers
Matches Law C to federalism
Names separation of powers and federalism, and says the chapter lists them as separate values

questions.q: Give one example each, from the later sections of the chapter, of 'executive accountability' and of 'financial accountability'.
questions.a: Executive accountability: the Question Hour, where MPs ask ministers about policies and activities, or special committees where ministries explain their policies. Financial accountability: examining the distribution of funds to different ministries, or the annual budget.
s: Gives a correct example of executive accountability
Gives a correct example of financial accountability

questions.q: How can the Council of Ministers be chosen from the MPs of both houses and yet be responsible to only one of them? Explain with the chapter's rule.
questions.a: The chapter says the Council is chosen from among the MPs of both houses, so a minister may sit in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. It then says the ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, which means the Council as a whole answers to that House whatever House a minister belongs to.
s: States that ministers are chosen from MPs of both houses
States that the responsibility is to the Lok Sabha
Explains that membership and responsibility are separate questions

questions.q: A draft poster says: 'The Parliament ensures federalism by keeping all power at the centre.' Show that this cannot be right, using the chapter's definition, and rewrite the line correctly.
questions.a: The chapter defines federalism as a form of government where power is distributed between the centre, states and local governments, and says it keeps the balance between national unity and local interests. Keeping all power at the centre is the opposite of distributing it. Corrected line: the Parliament ensures federalism by upholding a system in which power is distributed between the centre, states and local governments.
s: States the chapter's definition of federalism as distribution of power
Shows that all power at the centre contradicts it
Rewrites the line correctly

questions.q: A newspaper lists six events: (i) electing the President; (ii) passing a bill into an act; (iii) ministers justifying decisions in the first hour of a session; (iv) examining how funds are shared among ministries; (v) amending the Constitution; (vi) a special committee questioning a ministry. Sort them under the chapter's four heads and say what links events (iii) and (vi).
questions.a: Constitutional functions: (i) and (v). Lawmaking: (ii). Executive accountability: (iii) and (vi). Financial accountability: (iv). Events (iii) and (vi) are linked by being ways of making the Executive justify and explain its actions and decisions.
s: Places (i) and (v) under constitutional functions
Places (ii) under lawmaking
Places (iii) and (vi) under executive accountability
Places (iv) under financial accountability
Says what links (iii) and (vi): making the Executive explain its actions

questions.q: The chapter lists four core values that the Parliament is entrusted with upholding. (a) Which value does universal adult suffrage serve? (b) Which value does a law protecting Fundamental Rights serve?
questions.a: (a) Enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage. (b) Upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies.
s: Links universal adult suffrage to enabling parliamentary democracy
Links the law protecting Fundamental Rights to upholding Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles

questions.q: True or False? 'The Parliament's executive responsibility is less important than its legislative function, since laws are made first.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the executive responsibility, ensuring that laws are implemented and enforced, is as important as the legislative function, the making of laws.
s: Gives the verdict: false
Corrects it: the executive responsibility is as important as the legislative function

questions.q:
Sunita is an MP of the Rajya Sabha and has been made a minister in the Union Council of Ministers. A student calls this an anomaly, because the chapter says the Council is answerable to the Lok Sabha.
(a) Is Sunita's selection allowed by the chapter's rule?
(b) To which House is she, as a minister, collectively responsible?
(c) Explain why this is not an anomaly.
(d) The Council has 20 ministers, 6 of them from the Rajya Sabha (illustrative). If the Lok Sabha withdrew its support, how many of the 20 would be affected under the chapter's rule, and why?
questions.a: (a) Yes, the Council of Ministers is chosen from among the MPs of both houses. (b) The Lok Sabha. (c) The chapter separates where ministers are chosen from (both houses) from whom they answer to (the Lok Sabha), so a Rajya Sabha MP can be a minister while the Council answers to the Lok Sabha. (d) All 20, because the ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha as one Council, including the 6 from the Rajya Sabha.
s: Says the selection is allowed
Names the Lok Sabha
Explains the separation of where chosen from and to whom responsible
Says all 20 are affected, because responsibility is collective

questions.q: Hari says: 'The Parliament upholds Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies.' Test his statement.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter lists this as the fourth of the core values the Parliament is directly entrusted with upholding, and says it does so by framing laws and policies.
s: Gives the verdict: right
Says it is one of the four core values the Parliament upholds
Says the means is framing laws and policies

questions.q:
(a) Define the 'legislative' function and the 'executive' responsibility as the chapter uses the words.
(b) A law to supply free spectacles to schoolchildren is passed but no officer is told to carry it out. Which of the two has been left incomplete?
questions.a: (a) Legislative: the making of laws. Executive: ensuring that laws are implemented and enforced. (b) The executive responsibility.
s: Defines legislative as law-making and executive as implementing and enforcing laws
Names the executive responsibility as the one left incomplete

questions.q: A student says: 'The chapter lists every constitutional function of the Parliament.' What does the chapter actually say?
questions.a: It names the election of the President and Vice President and amendments, and leaves other functions to higher grades
o: It names the election of the President and Vice President and amendments, and leaves other functions to higher grades
It names only the election of the President, and says amendments to the Constitution belong to the Executive
It names every constitutional function in full and says that none remain to be explored in higher grades
It names amendments and lawmaking, and says that the election of the Vice President belongs to the Judiciary

questions.q: Which of these is NOT among the four core values that the Parliament is directly entrusted with upholding?
questions.a: Approving and monitoring government expenditure through the annual budget
o: Approving and monitoring government expenditure through the annual budget
Following the separation of powers among legislature, executive and judiciary
Ensuring federalism
Upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies

questions.q: Design a poster called 'Four Promises of Parliament' with one box for each core constitutional value the chapter says the Parliament is entrusted with upholding. In each box write the value in the chapter's words and one line saying how a law or policy could serve it, and add a closing line on the head of functions under which the chapter lists them.
questions.a: Box 1: enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage, for example a law keeping the vote open to every adult. Box 2: following the separation of powers between legislature, executive and judiciary, for example a law that keeps each organ to its own role. Box 3: ensuring federalism, for example a policy that shares responsibilities between centre and states. Box 4: upholding Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy by framing laws and policies, for example a law on free schooling. Closing line: these fall under the Parliament's constitutional functions.
s: States value 1 with a fitting example
States value 2 with a fitting example
States value 3 with a fitting example
States value 4 with a fitting example
Names constitutional functions as the head

questions.q:
Match each term of lawmaking in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Reading  2. Clause  3. Gazette  4. Standing Committee
Column B: a. an official government publication that announces legal documents  b. a permanent committee of MPs that scrutinises government activities  c. a part of a bill explaining a specific detail, such as the age group of RTE  d. a stage that began when a clerk read out the bill for MPs who could not read

Assertion (A): A bill must always be introduced first in the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education bill was tabled in the Rajya Sabha.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
A website's timeline of RTE says: 'RTE began as a bill in the Lok Sabha in 2008. Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002, covers children between 6 and 14. No committee examined it. It received the President's assent in August 2009.'
(a) Which two statements of the timeline are wrong?
(b) Correct each of them.
(c) Which two statements are reliable?
(d) The site says the bill began in the Lok Sabha. If that were so, going by the flowchart's step 'process repeated in other House', which House would have taken it up second, and which House does the chapter say took it up first?
questions.a: (a) 'Began as a bill in the Lok Sabha' and 'No committee examined it'. (b) The bill was tabled in the Rajya Sabha; a committee studied it thoroughly and suggested modifications. (c) The statement on Article 21A and ages 6 to 14, and the assent in August 2009. (d) The Rajya Sabha would have come second; the chapter says the Rajya Sabha took it first, and the Lok Sabha passed it later, in August 2009.
s: Identifies the two wrong statements
Corrects the House and the committee
Names the Article 21A and the assent statements as reliable
Says the Rajya Sabha would be second on the site's version, but the chapter has it first

questions.q: The flowchart carries the note 'All bills may not be referred to Committees'. What does this tell a reader about the steps of the flowchart, and which step does it affect?
questions.a: It tells the reader that the flowchart is a simplified diagram of key steps and that a bill may skip the step of being referred to a Standing Committee; the other steps still follow.
s: Says some bills may not go to a committee
Identifies the Standing Committee referral as the step affected

questions.q: A student asks why the stage in which MPs take up a bill is called 'reading', when today MPs read the bill themselves before the discussions. Which explanation does the chapter support?
questions.a: The term began in the British Parliament, where a clerk read bills aloud for MPs who could not read
o: The term began in the British Parliament, where a clerk read bills aloud for MPs who could not read
The term began in the Constituent Assembly, where each clause was read aloud by the Speaker to the members
The term began with the Standing Committee, whose members read the bill to the minister
The term began in the Gazette, which prints every bill so that citizens can read it

questions.q:
Two bills are before Parliament in an imagined case. Bill X (illustrative) raises a tax on tea and fixes the amount the government may borrow this year. Bill Y proposes new rules for school bus safety and is not concerned with taxation or borrowing. An MP of the Rajya Sabha wants to introduce both bills in her House.
(a) Can she introduce Bill X in the Rajya Sabha?
(b) What must come before the introduction of Bill X in its House?
(c) Can she introduce Bill Y in the Rajya Sabha, and which step of the flowchart follows its vote there?
(d) In which House does each bill start, and so which bill reaches the Rajya Sabha first?
questions.a: (a) No: a Money Bill, concerned with taxation and government borrowing, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. (b) The President's prior recommendation. (c) Yes, a bill can be introduced in either House; the process is then repeated in the other House. (d) Bill X starts in the Lok Sabha and Bill Y can start in the Rajya Sabha, so Bill Y is the one that reaches the Rajya Sabha first.
s: Says Bill X cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha
Names the President's prior recommendation
Says Bill Y can start in the Rajya Sabha and the process then repeats in the other House
Says Bill X starts in the Lok Sabha and Bill Y can start in the Rajya Sabha, so Y reaches it first

questions.q: RTE was tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha six years after the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, that is, in the year ___.
(a) What is a bill? (b) What does an act do, and why do the two words differ?
questions.a: (a) A draft of a proposed law that needs Parliament's approval before it can be enacted into law. (b) An act is the instrument through which a law is generally brought into force; a bill is only a proposal, an act is what a bill becomes after the journey.
s: Defines a bill as a draft needing Parliament's approval
Says an act is what brings a law into force, the result of a bill's journey

questions.q: (Assume, for this question, that the flowchart's nine steps run in this order: introduction in either House; reading of the bill; referral to a Standing Committee; taken up for consideration and passing; clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted; vote on the bill; process repeated in the other House; presidential assent; gazette notification.) Show that, on this order, a bill cannot become an act on the day it is voted in the first House.
questions.a: After the vote in one House the process is repeated in the other House, so a second House must also take it up. Presidential assent comes after that, and a gazette notification follows. So the vote in the first House leaves at least these later steps undone.
s: Names the repetition of the process in the other House
Names presidential assent and gazette notification as later steps
Concludes that the first House's vote cannot complete the journey

questions.q:
(a) Which Article did the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 mandate, and for which children?
(b) RTE became an Act in August 2009. How many years after the amendment is that?
questions.a: (a) Article 21A, mandating that the state provide free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of 6 and 14 years. (b) 2009 - 2002 = 7 years.
s: Names Article 21A and children between 6 and 14
Works out 7 years

questions.q: A bill proposes a new tax and a rise in government borrowing (illustrative). A Rajya Sabha MP wants to introduce it there. What does the chapter say?
questions.a: It is a Money Bill: only the Lok Sabha may introduce it, and only on the President's prior recommendation
o: It is a Money Bill: only the Lok Sabha may introduce it, and only on the President's prior recommendation
It can be introduced in either House, but only with the President's prior recommendation
It can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha, since the Council of States represents the states that raise taxes
It can be introduced in the Lok Sabha without any recommendation, since the Lok Sabha is directly elected

questions.q: Divya says: 'The Constitution makers wanted RTE implemented within a decade after Independence, and that is exactly what happened.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the Constitution makers wanted the right implemented within a decade after Independence, so the first part is correct. But it adds that this did not happen, leaving countless children without access to education; RTE came into existence only in August 2009.
s: Gives the verdict: partly right
Confirms that the makers wanted it within a decade
Corrects the second part: it did not happen, and RTE came in August 2009

questions.q: (Assume, for this question, that the flowchart's nine steps run in this order: introduction in either House; reading of the bill; referral to a Standing Committee; taken up for consideration and passing; clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted; vote on the bill; process repeated in the other House; presidential assent; gazette notification.) A student arranges four of these steps. Which arrangement is in the right order?
questions.a: Reading of the bill, referral to a Standing Committee, clause-by-clause discussion, presidential assent
o: Reading of the bill, referral to a Standing Committee, clause-by-clause discussion, presidential assent
Reading of the bill, clause-by-clause discussion, presidential assent, referral to a Standing Committee
Presidential assent, reading of the bill, referral to a Standing Committee, clause-by-clause discussion
Referral to a Standing Committee, reading of the bill, presidential assent, clause-by-clause discussion

questions.q: A bill contains the line 'This Act applies to children between the ages of 6 and 14 years.' Which part of a bill, in the chapter's terms, is this line?
questions.a: A clause, which explains a specific detail of the bill
o: A clause, which explains a specific detail of the bill
A reading, which is the stage when the bill is read before discussion
A gazette, which announces the bill as an official publication
A Standing Committee, which scrutinises the bill

questions.q: A Class 5 student asks, 'How does an idea become a law?' (Assume, for this question, that the flowchart's nine steps run in this order: introduction in either House; reading of the bill; referral to a Standing Committee; taken up for consideration and passing; clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted; vote on the bill; process repeated in the other House; presidential assent; gazette notification.) Group the nine steps into three named stages of your own choice and say which steps go in each and why.
questions.a: Sample grouping (any consistent grouping with reasons earns the marks): Stage 1, Starting: introduction, reading, referral to a Standing Committee if sent. Stage 2, Debating: consideration and passing, clause-by-clause discussion, the vote. Stage 3, Finishing: the process repeated in the other House, presidential assent, gazette notification. Each stage has a single purpose: opening the bill, testing it, making it official.
s: Names three stages
Places every one of the nine steps in some stage, leaving none out
Keeps the steps in the assumed order within and across the stages
Gives a reason for the first stage's grouping
Gives a reason for the other two groupings

questions.q: A villager asks why education counts as a right and not just a service. Using the early-1990s court argument in the RTE story, (a) name the Fundamental Right that was said to include it, and (b) give the reason the argument offered.
questions.a: (a) The Right to Life. (b) Education is important to lead a meaningful life, so it was said to be inherently part of that right.
s: Names the Right to Life
Gives the reason: education is important to lead a meaningful life

questions.q:
Read the statements about lawmaking.
(I) A Standing Committee is a permanent committee whose MPs can never change.
(II) A bill needs the Parliament's approval before it can be enacted into law.
(III) An act is generally the instrument through which a law is brought into force.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I only
I, II and III

questions.q: Which of these statements does NOT agree with the chapter's account of lawmaking?
questions.a: Every bill must be referred to a Standing Committee before it is taken up for consideration
o: Every bill must be referred to a Standing Committee before it is taken up for consideration
After a bill is voted in one House, the process is repeated in the other House
A bill is a draft of a proposed law that needs Parliament's approval before it can be enacted
A law is generally brought into force through an instrument called an act

questions.q: Arrange these RTE events in order and give the year or gap the chapter gives: (i) the bill is passed in the Lok Sabha and gets the President's assent; (ii) the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act; (iii) a court is told that education is part of the Right to Life; (iv) the bill is tabled in the Rajya Sabha and a committee studies it. Then name the issue the chapter says was the major debate.
questions.a: (iii) Early 1990s: someone argued in court that education is part of the Right to Life. (ii) 2002: the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act mandated Article 21A. (iv) Six years later: the bill was tabled in the Rajya Sabha and a committee studied it. (i) August 2009: passed in the Lok Sabha and received the President's assent. The major debate concerned funding: new schools, infrastructure and teachers would be costly.
s: Places the court argument first with the early 1990s
Places the 86th Amendment second with 2002
Places the tabling in the Rajya Sabha and committee third, six years later
Places passage in the Lok Sabha and assent last, August 2009
Names funding as the major debate

questions.q: (Assume, for this question, that the flowchart's nine steps run in this order: introduction in either House; reading of the bill; referral to a Standing Committee; taken up for consideration and passing; clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted; vote on the bill; process repeated in the other House; presidential assent; gazette notification.) RTE was tabled in the Rajya Sabha. Using the flowchart, say what the process would be if a bill like it were tabled in the Lok Sabha instead, and say which steps would not change.
questions.a: It would be introduced in the Lok Sabha, then be read, perhaps be referred to a Standing Committee, taken up for consideration and passing, discussed clause by clause with amendments voted, and voted on. The process would then be repeated in the Rajya Sabha, followed by presidential assent and gazette notification. By the flowchart, the steps themselves do not change, only which House goes first.
s: Starts with introduction in the Lok Sabha
Has the process repeated in the Rajya Sabha afterwards
Says the steps stay the same and only the order of the Houses changes

questions.q: (Assume, for this question, that the flowchart's nine steps run in this order: introduction in either House; reading of the bill; referral to a Standing Committee; taken up for consideration and passing; clause-by-clause discussion with amendments voted; vote on the bill; process repeated in the other House; presidential assent; gazette notification.) A bill has been voted in both Houses. (a) On this order, which step comes next? (b) Which step then announces it as an official publication?
questions.a: (a) Presidential assent. (b) Gazette notification.
s: Names presidential assent
Names gazette notification, the official announcement

questions.q: A report says: 'The Standing Committee ordered the Ministry of Ayush to open a Department of Ayush in every State and UT.' The Committee's recommendation reads: 'recommends the Ministry of Ayush to impress upon and persuade the States and UTs with no separate department of Ayush to create such a department'. Which correction fits, given the chapter's account of what a Standing Committee does?
questions.a: A Standing Committee makes recommendations, and here it recommended that the Ministry persuade the States and UTs to act
o: A Standing Committee makes recommendations, and here it recommended that the Ministry persuade the States and UTs to act
A Standing Committee passes laws, and here it passed a law requiring every State and UT to create the departments
A Standing Committee appoints ministers, and here it appointed a new Minister of Ayush for the States and UTs
A Standing Committee sanctions expenses, and here it sanctioned funds for new departments in every State and UT

questions.q: A ministry's spending report reaches Parliament late and with a wrong total. Write the two-line recommendation (illustrative) that a Committee might make, and the two-line reply the ministry might give, so that the chapter's expectation of timely and accurate information is spelled out.
questions.a: Sample. Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the ministry submit its spending reports to Parliament on time and ensure that totals match the details. Reply: The ministry will submit future reports within the scheduled time, and its accounts section will check every total before submission.
s: Writes a recommendation that names both timely and accurate
Writes a reply that answers the recommendation
Keeps the pattern of Recommendation and Action Taken

questions.q:
(a) On what occasion did Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman recite a verse from the Tirukkural?
(b) What does the verse say citizens live expecting, and to what does it compare this?
questions.a: (a) While presenting the Union Budget for 2025-26 on 1 February 2025. (b) Citizens live expecting good governance, just as living beings live expecting rains.
s: Names the Union Budget for 2025-26 on 1 February 2025
Gives the meaning: citizens expect good governance

questions.q: Zoya says: 'Special committees are made only of MPs of the ruling party, so they cannot hold a ministry to account.' Test her claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the committees may include MPs from different political parties, so 'only the ruling party' is not what it says, and the claim also overlooks that ministries have to explain and answer questions about their policies at the meetings, which is how they are held to account.
s: Gives the verdict: not correct
Cites that committees may include MPs from different parties
Says the ministries must explain and answer questions there

questions.q:
The chapter says its extract is from the report of meetings between the Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare and the officers of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Item 1.2 of the report, on the co-location of Ayush facilities, reads: 'Recommendation: ... recommends the Ministry of Ayush to impress upon and persuade the States and UTs with no separate department of Ayush to create such a department ...' and 'Action Taken: Public Health is being a state subject, creation of separate Department of Ayush ... comes under purview of respective State/UT Governments. However, Ministry of Ayush has requested State/UT Governments ... to create separate Directorates ... As on date, separate Ayush Directorate is available in 24 States/UTs.'
(a) Using the chapter's definition of a Standing Committee, say what kind of body this Committee is and what it does with government activities.
(b) Using the chapter's meaning of 'accountable', say who is being made to justify what, and to whom.
(c) Did the Ministry of Ayush itself create the departments the Committee wanted? Answer from the Action Taken.
(d) Using the chapter's definition of federalism, say what the reply shows about the Union ministry and the States.
(e) By the chapter's meaning of 'accountable', is the reply an example of the Executive being accountable? Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) A permanent committee of MPs (the MPs may change, the committee as a structure remains) that scrutinises government activities, makes recommendations and asks questions on actions taken by the government. (b) The Ministry, through its officers, must justify its actions and decisions to the Committee of MPs. (c) No: it said creation rests with the State and UT governments and that it had only requested them to act. (d) Federalism is power distributed between the centre, states and local governments; the Union ministry can request the States, which hold the power to create the departments. (e) Yes, by the chapter's meaning (justifying actions and decisions): the ministry gave a reason (public health is a state subject), reported its action (requests) and a figure (24 States/UTs).
s: Defines a Standing Committee: permanent, of MPs, scrutinises, recommends, asks questions
Says the ministry must justify its actions to the Committee, using 'accountable'
Says the Ministry did not create them itself; it requested the States/UTs
Links to federalism: power distributed, so the Union can only request
Gives the verdict yes, with reason, action and figure

questions.q: The chapter says the government is expected to give Parliament information 'in a timely and accurate manner'. Explain with one example how late information and wrong information would each weaken financial accountability.
questions.a: Late information: if figures on spending reach Parliament after the budget has already been spent, it cannot examine the distribution of funds when it matters. Wrong information: if a ministry's total is wrong, Parliament would approve and monitor expenditure on a false picture.
s: Explains the effect of late information
Explains the effect of wrong information

questions.q: After a new Lok Sabha is constituted, several MPs on a Standing Committee are replaced. Does the Standing Committee, as the chapter defines it, cease to exist?
questions.a: No, because the MPs may change but the committee as a structure remains
o: No, because the MPs may change but the committee as a structure remains
Yes, because a Standing Committee is made of particular MPs and ends when they leave
Yes, because Standing Committees are formed afresh for each bill
No, because a Standing Committee has the same MPs for as long as the Parliament lasts

questions.q:
A school magazine writes: 'Parliament is always formal and serious. No verse or humour is ever heard in it. For example, a Union Budget speech has no room for poetry.' The editor offers to change 'always' to 'often' and keep the rest.
(a) Which example from the chapter contradicts the claim about the Budget speech, and on what date?
(b) Which second example, from a Lok Sabha debate, contradicts 'no verse is ever heard'?
(c) What does the chapter itself say about the atmosphere in Parliament?
(d) Does changing 'always' to 'often' alone make the magazine's sentence agree with the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman recited a Tirukkural verse while presenting the Union Budget for 2025-26 on 1 February 2025. (b) The 2011 exchange in which Sushma Swaraj quoted a poetic verse and Dr. Manmohan Singh replied with another line. (c) That Parliament isn't always formal and serious; sometimes the atmosphere is set through poetry and humour. (d) No: the sentences 'no verse or humour is ever heard' and 'a Budget speech has no room for poetry' are still wrong, so the magazine must change those as well.
s: Names the Tirukkural verse in the Budget speech on 1 February 2025
Names the 2011 exchange between Sushma Swaraj and Dr. Manmohan Singh
States the chapter's remark that Parliament isn't always formal and serious
Says changing 'always' alone is not enough since the other claims are also wrong

questions.q: True or False? 'A special committee in which MPs of several parties sit can still make a ministry explain and answer questions about its policies.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says special committees hold meetings where ministries have to explain and answer questions about their policies, and that these committees may include MPs from different political parties.
s: Gives the verdict: true
Gives the support: ministries must explain and answer, whatever the parties of the MPs

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Special committees may include MPs from different political parties.
Reason (R): Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman recited a Tirukkural verse while presenting the Union Budget for 2025-26.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Officers of a ministry attend a meeting where MPs of three different parties question them about the ministry's policies, and the officers must answer. Whose accountability does this meeting show, and to whom?
questions.a: The Executive's accountability, to MPs of the Parliament
o: The Executive's accountability, to MPs of the Parliament
The Legislature's accountability, to the ministry's officers

questions.q: An MP asks a minister in the first hour of a session why a scheme has been delayed, and the minister has to give reasons. Which process of the Parliament is this, and what does it do?
questions.a: The Question Hour, which holds the Executive accountable by making it justify its actions
o: The Question Hour, which holds the Executive accountable by making it justify its actions
The Question Hour, which lets the Legislature take over the work of implementing laws
A Standing Committee, which passes a bill clause by clause and sends it to the President
The annual budget, which approves the expenditure of the ministries and examines their funds

questions.q: The chapter gives the Parliament three tools to hold the Executive and the money of government to account: the Question Hour, special committees and the annual budget. (a) Describe each in one line. (b) Say which of the three speaks directly of money. (c) Say which of the three the chapter ties to a set time in a session, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The Question Hour: in the first hour MPs ask ministers about policies and activities. Special committees: ministries explain and answer questions about their policies at their meetings. questions.q: Define a Standing Committee as the chapter does, explain what 'the MPs may change, but the committee as a structure remains' means, and name one thing it does.

s: Defines it as a permanent committee of MPs

questions.q: (a) What must ministries do at the meetings of special committees? (b) Why might it matter that a committee may include MPs from different political parties? Answer with one reason of your own.

Gives a reasoned point about MPs of different parties

questions.q:
A discussion in Parliament in an imagined year (illustrative) covers the distribution of Rs 50,000 crore among three ministries: Health Rs 12,000 crore, Education Rs 18,000 crore and Transport Rs 20,000 crore. Health sends its spending report on time and its total matches its parts. Transport sends its report on time, but its total is Rs 500 crore more than the sum of its parts. Education sends its detailed report five weeks late, and its total is Rs 2,000 crore less than the sum of its parts. The committee has time to question only one ministry first.
(a) Under which of the four functions does this examination fall?
(b) What percentage of Education's Rs 18,000 crore is the Rs 2,000 crore discrepancy, to one decimal place?
(c) Which of the chapter's two expectations about information does each of the three ministries meet or fail?
(d) Which ministry should the committee question first, and why?
questions.a: (a) Financial accountability. (b) 2,000/18,000 x 100 = 11.1 per cent. (c) Health meets both the timely and the accurate expectation; Transport is timely but not accurate; Education fails both, being late and having a wrong total. (d) Education, because it fails both expectations, while Transport fails only one and Health none.
s: Names financial accountability
Computes 11.1 per cent
States Health meets both, Transport only one, Education neither
Chooses Education because it fails both expectations

questions.q: In 2011, a spirited Lok Sabha debate saw an exchange of poetic lines. (a) Who quoted a verse to criticise the government, and who replied? (b) What was the point of the first verse, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: (a) Sushma Swaraj quoted the verse, and the then Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh replied with another poetic line. (b) That the speaker should not change the topic but say why the caravan was looted: the question was on the leadership.
s: Names Sushma Swaraj and Dr. Manmohan Singh
Gives the point: a question on leadership, not a change of topic

Ravi is performing executive accountability and Sana financial accountability

A verse recited in the Parliament replaces the need for any debate on the matter at hand

questions.q: (a) Whom does the Council of Ministers aid and advise, according to the chapter? (b) To which House is the Council collectively responsible?
questions.a: (a) The President. (b) The Lok Sabha.

Names two independence rows

Gives a reasoned judgement on dependence and independence

questions.q: After a Lok Sabha election, no party holds a clear majority. According to the chapter, which statement about the President's role fits this situation?

questions.a: The President is the Head of State and the nominal head of the Executive, who appoints the Prime Minister and ministers, summons the Parliament and gives assent to bills. Describes the Prime Minister as the de facto executive authority

questions.q:
In one session of an imagined Parliament (illustrative), 30 bills were introduced: 25 by ministers of the government and 5 by other MPs. Someone concludes: 'Since most bills come from the Executive, the Legislature has no control over what the Executive does.'
(a) Does the 25 of 30 agree with the chapter's statement about who introduces most bills?

Rejects the conclusion using those two checks

questions.q: In her first week a new Prime Minister (illustrative) does four things: (i) briefs the President on a crisis; (ii) settles a dispute between the Railways and Steel ministries over a siding; (iii) announces a new national policy on school meals; (iv) chairs the meeting of her Council of Ministers. (a) Match each event to one of the chapter's four key functions of the Prime Minister. (b) Name the House to which she and her Council are collectively responsible.
questions.a: (a) (i) Advising the President; (ii) coordinating the work of different ministries; (iii) shaping national policies; (iv) leading the Council of Ministers. (b) The Lok Sabha.

Matches (ii) to coordinating ministries

A minister is answerable to the Rajya Sabha for every accident in the whole country
A minister must resign whenever the Prime Minister declines her proposal in the Council
A minister is a civil servant and must accept blame on behalf of the officials

questions.q: Show that, by the chapter's rule, the leader of the party with the most members in the Rajya Sabha cannot be appointed Prime Minister merely because of that.
questions.a: The chapter says the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha as the Prime Minister. It also says the Prime Minister serves with the support of the majority of the MPs in the Lok Sabha. Strength in the Rajya Sabha appears in neither rule, so it cannot decide the appointment.

States that the Prime Minister serves with the support of a Lok Sabha majority

questions.q:

questions.a: (a) The Legislature sanctions all government-related expenses; the Executive prepares and implements the budget approved by Parliament. (b) The Executive can implement only the budget that the Parliament has approved, and the Parliament relies on the Executive to carry it out.

Explains that the two depend on each other

questions.q:
In an imagined Lok Sabha election (illustrative), no single party wins a clear majority. Coalition K, made up of three parties, shows the President that the majority of the Lok Sabha's MPs support its leader, Ms Devi. Party L is the single largest party but has fewer MPs than the three parties of Coalition K together.
(a) Which situation named in the chapter does this election fit, and what power may the President use in it?
(b) Whom does the chapter's rule say the President appoints as Prime Minister, and why?
(c) To which House is her Council of Ministers collectively responsible?
(d) Some months later, the MPs backing Coalition K fall below a majority of the Lok Sabha. Which condition of the chapter for serving as Prime Minister is no longer met?
questions.a: (a) The situation in which no party holds a clear majority in a Lok Sabha election, in which the President may exercise discretionary powers. (b) Ms Devi, the leader of the coalition with majority support in the Lok Sabha. (c) The Lok Sabha. (d) The Prime Minister serves with the support of the majority of the MPs in the Lok Sabha, and that support is gone.
s: Names no clear majority as the circumstance
Names Ms Devi as leader of the coalition with majority support
Names the Lok Sabha
Says the support of a majority of Lok Sabha MPs is missing

questions.q: The chapter's example of a Railway Minister who resigned after a train accident, though he was not blamed for it, dates from the year ___.

A student's answer on the Shastri account reads: 'Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned in 1956 because an inquiry blamed him for a train accident. Prime Minister Nehru accepted the resignation at once. This shows that every minister must resign when anything goes wrong in a ministry.' Her teacher asks the class to examine it.
(a) Which details of the answer contradict the chapter?
(b) What did Shastri himself believe?
(c) What happened between Nehru and Shastri over the resignation?
(d) Two readings of the chapter: Reading 1, 'the chapter lays down that every minister must resign when anything goes wrong'; Reading 2, 'the chapter reports that Shastri himself believed a minister must take moral responsibility'. Which reading matches the chapter's wording, and which word shows it?
questions.a: (a) He was not blamed for the accident, and Nehru did not accept at once. (b) That a minister must take moral responsibility for anything that happens in their ministry. (c) Nehru declined at first, Shastri insisted and finally the resignation was accepted. (d) Reading 2: the chapter says he believed this, so the word 'believed' shows it is Shastri's own view and not a rule laid down for every minister.
s: Names the two contradicting details
States Shastri's belief about moral responsibility
Gives Nehru declining at first and Shastri insisting
Chooses Reading 2 and points to the word 'believed'

questions.q: Nisha says: 'Civil servants work under the direction of ministers and help implement laws and policies, and they form a permanent group.' Test her statement.

Confirms that they are a permanent group

questions.q:
Match each person or group in Column A with the description in Column B.

(a) Name two things the President does, as the chapter lists them. (b) According to the comparison table, who aids and advises the President on important matters, including calling sessions of Parliament?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers, summons the Parliament, gives assent to bills. (b) The Executive, through the Council of Ministers.
