questions.q: (a) According to the comparison table, who introduces most of the bills in Parliament, and what can the Legislature itself introduce? (b) Why does the table say the Executive 'provides information and explanations to the Legislature'?
questions.a: (a) Most of the bills are introduced by the Executive; the Legislature can introduce some bills. (b) Because the Legislature keeps a check on the Executive by asking questions and seeking explanations, and the Executive must answer them.
s: Says most bills come from the Executive and the Legislature introduces some
Links the Executive's explanations to the Legislature's questions

questions.q: According to the chapter's comparison table, which of these is done by the Executive and not by the Legislature?
questions.a: Preparing and implementing the budget approved by Parliament
o: Preparing and implementing the budget approved by Parliament
Asking questions and seeking explanations about the Executive's actions
Sanctioning all government-related expenses
Keeping a check on the activities of the Executive

questions.q: The chapter says the Judiciary interprets and applies laws 'including in specific cases of disputes'. (a) Which organ makes the laws and which organ carries them out? (b) How does the Judiciary's work on a dispute differ from both?
questions.a: (a) The Legislature makes the laws and the Executive carries them out. (b) The Judiciary interprets and applies the laws to the specific dispute, resolving it, instead of making or enforcing the law.
s: Names the Legislature and the Executive correctly
Says the Judiciary interprets and applies laws to resolve a dispute

questions.q:
In an imagined country (illustrative), four incidents occur in one month.
Incident 1: MPs ask a minister why a rural scheme has been delayed, and she must explain.
Incident 2: A court finds that a ministry's order, issued to carry out a law, violates the Constitution, and steps in.
Incident 3: The Parliament passes a new law.
Incident 4: A ministry issues instructions to carry out an earlier law.
(a) Which incident shows the Legislature checking the Executive?
(b) Which shows the Judiciary checking the Executive?
(c) Which two incidents are the making and the implementing of laws?
(d) Incidents 1 and 2 are both checks on the Executive. How do they differ in who checks and on what ground?
questions.a: (a) Incident 1. (b) Incident 2. (c) Incident 3, the making of a law by the Legislature, and Incident 4, its implementation by the Executive. (d) In Incident 1 the Legislature checks by asking questions and seeking explanations; in Incident 2 the Judiciary checks whether the Executive's action respects the Constitution.
s: Picks Incident 1
Picks Incident 2
Picks Incidents 3 and 4
Contrasts the Legislature's questions and explanations with the Judiciary's check against the Constitution

questions.q: A teacher explains to a student, in two or three sentences of dialogue, how the three organs stop one another from becoming too powerful. Write the dialogue (illustrative), using one check by the Legislature and one by the Judiciary.
questions.a: Sample. Student: Who stops the Executive from going too far? Teacher: The Legislature questions it and seeks explanations, and the Judiciary can step in if the Constitution is violated when a law is implemented. Student: And the Legislature? Teacher: The Judiciary checks that laws passed by Parliament have not violated the Constitutional framework, so no one organ becomes too powerful.
s: Gives a check by the Legislature on the Executive
Gives a check by the Judiciary
Links the checks to no organ becoming too powerful

questions.q: A citizen believes that a law passed by Parliament violates the Constitutional framework. According to the chapter, which organ has been given the responsibility of checking this?
questions.a: The Judiciary, through its system of courts
o: The Judiciary, through its system of courts
The Executive, through the Council of Ministers
The Legislature, through its Speaker
The President, as Head of State

questions.q: The chapter says the Constitution lists the specific responsibilities of the Legislature and the Executive and gives the Judiciary a 'unique and critical responsibility'. Explain what the responsibility is and why it follows from the Constitution listing the responsibilities of the other two.
questions.a: The responsibility is checking that the laws passed by Parliament have not violated the Constitutional framework, and stepping in if the Executive violates it while implementing laws. It follows because once the Constitution sets down what the Legislature and the Executive may do, someone has to see that they stay within it, and the Judiciary does so.
s: States the responsibility of checking laws and implementation against the Constitution
Notes that the Constitution lists the responsibilities of the Legislature and the Executive
Links the two: the listed limits need an organ to enforce them

questions.q: Which example below shows the Legislature checking the Executive, as opposed to the Judiciary checking another organ?
questions.a: MPs asking ministers questions about their policies in the Question Hour

A court stepping in when the Executive's implementation of a law violates the Constitution
The Executive preparing and implementing the budget that Parliament has approved

questions.q: State the closing point of the chapter for each organ: (a) the Legislature, (b) the Executive, (c) the Judiciary. Then say in a line why the chapter ends with all three.
questions.a: (a) Makes laws. (b) Implements them. (c) Ensures that they follow the Constitution. All three are needed so that making, carrying out and checking of laws are separate and no organ becomes too powerful.
s: Gives Legislature as making laws, Executive as implementing and Judiciary as ensuring they follow the Constitution
Gives the reason that no one organ should become too powerful

Universal adult franchise, so that every adult citizen can vote
Federalism, so that power is shared between the centre and the states
A bicameral Parliament, so that a second House can review the first

questions.a: Preparing and implementing the budget
o: Preparing and implementing the budget
Interpreting the laws of the land
Resolving disputes between parties

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter mean when it calls the Judiciary 'the custodian of the Constitution'?
(b) Name one thing the Judiciary checks in each of the other two organs.
questions.a: (a) It ensures that all branches of the government operate within the principles and parameters enshrined in the Constitution. (b) In the Legislature, that the laws passed by Parliament have not violated the Constitutional framework; in the Executive, that a law is not implemented in violation of the Constitution.

Names a check on the Legislature and a check on the Executive

questions.q:
Law H (illustrative) is passed by an imagined Parliament and is carried out by the Executive in 14 districts. In 3 districts, the manner of carrying it out violates the Constitution. No one has said that the text of Law H itself breaks the Constitutional framework.

questions.a: (a) 3/14 x 100 = 21.4 per cent. (b) The Judiciary. (c) No: the stem reports violations only in 3 districts. (d) No: the chapter gives the Judiciary two separate checks, one on the laws passed by Parliament and one on violations when laws are implemented by the Executive, and the stem reports only violations in implementation.
s: Computes 21.4 per cent
Names the Judiciary
Says there is no reported violation in the other 11
Says the two checks are separate and only implementation is in question

questions.q: Explain how the three organs check one another, using (a) how the Legislature checks the Executive, (b) how the Judiciary checks the Legislature, (c) how the Judiciary checks the Executive, (d) the term the chapter uses for the whole arrangement and (e) the purpose it serves.
questions.a: (a) The Legislature asks questions and seeks explanations from the Executive, as in the Question Hour. (b) The Judiciary checks that laws passed by Parliament have not violated the Constitutional framework. (c) If a violation occurs when the Executive implements laws, the Judiciary has the power to step in. (d) Separation of powers and the system of checks and balances. (e) It ensures that no one organ becomes too powerful.
s: Explains the Legislature's check on the Executive
Explains the Judiciary's check on laws
Explains the Judiciary's check on implementation
Names separation of powers and checks and balances
States the purpose

questions.q: A student says, 'Courts apply laws, so they belong to the Executive.' How does the chapter place the courts?

Courts are a wing of the Parliament, which functions through its Legislature, Executive and Judiciary arms
Courts are part of the Council of Ministers, which interprets laws for the Prime Minister
Courts belong to the Legislature, since the Legislature makes the laws that courts apply

questions.q: A ministry carries out a law in a way that breaks the Constitution. According to the chapter, what can the Judiciary do?

o: Step in, because a violation of the Constitution when laws are implemented is also within its power to check
Nothing, because the Judiciary can check only the laws passed by Parliament and not how they are carried out by the Executive
Pass a new law, because the Judiciary functions through the same arms as the Parliament does

questions.q: Gita says: 'On a Concurrent List subject, both the Union and the state may make laws, and if the two differ the state's law prevails.' Test her claim.

Names Union List and Concurrent List for Parliament

Work out the mean of the four, and explain why the mean of the four lowest sessions can be below the lowest year's figure.
questions.a: Mean = (6.80 + 27.30 + 28.90 + 29.55)/4 = 92.55/4 = 23.14 per cent. A year's figure combines all the sessions in it, including better ones, so it can stay above the mean of the four poorest sessions.
s: Computes about 23.14 per cent
Says a year's figure combines several sessions
Explains that better sessions pull the year above the four lowest sessions' mean

Says the table gives only sessions and sittings

Venkaiah Naidu said the Rajya Sabha's productivity was about 78 per cent in 2004-14 and 'declined to about 65%' since then, and gave four low sessions of 6.80, 27.30, 28.90 and 29.55 per cent among 11. A student concludes: 'So every session after 2014 was at 65 per cent.' (a) Is that what the statement says? (b) What do the four low sessions show about the sessions?
questions.a: (a) No: 65 per cent is the figure for the period since 2014 taken together, not the figure for every session. (b) That sessions differed widely: four of the 11 were far below 65 per cent, between 6.80 and 29.55 per cent, so the overall figure combines high and low sessions.
s: Says 65 per cent is the figure for the whole period, not each session
Says the four low sessions show wide differences between sessions

Corrects it: hours actually functioned against hours scheduled

(b) For example: enacting laws, overseeing administrative processes, approving the budget, and platform for discussing policies and public grievances. (c) Angry or biased debates that do not seriously address people's issues, and the reduced quality of important debates. (d) That the Rajya Sabha's productivity fell from about 78 to about 65 per cent, with its lowest ever year at 35.75 per cent. (e) Productivity is a useful but not a sufficient measure: it shows hours but not the quality of debates, which the chapter treats as a separate concern.
s: States what productivity measures
Names roles of the legislature not seen in hours
Names two concerns about the debates themselves
Names what the Rajya Sabha data shows
Judges that hours are useful but not sufficient, with the quality-of-debate reason

questions.q:
M. Venkaiah Naidu stated in 2021 that the Rajya Sabha's productivity during 2004-14 had been about 78 per cent and had declined to about 65 per cent since then. Of the 11 sessions he presided over, four recorded 6.80, 27.30, 28.90 and 29.55 per cent, and in 2018 the House recorded its lowest ever productivity of 35.75 per cent.

(b) What percentage of the 11 sessions were among the four low ones, to one decimal place?
(c) Which two periods do the 78 per cent and the 65 per cent figures refer to?

questions.a: (a) The number of hours the House actually functioned against the time it was scheduled to. (b) 4/11 x 100 = 36.4 per cent. (c) 78 per cent refers to 2004-14 and 65 per cent to the period since then. (d) No: the passage gives about 65 per cent as the figure since 2014 and 35.75 per cent as the lowest ever year, but no year-by-year figures, so a fall in every year cannot be shown.

Computes 36.4 per cent
Names the two periods
Says no, because the passage gives no year-by-year figures

questions.q:
A State Assembly in an imagined case (illustrative) was scheduled for a short special series of 20 sittings of 6 hours each, 120 hours in all, and functioned for 78 hours. It wants to match the 78 per cent that the chapter gives for the Rajya Sabha in 2004-14 in a similar series next time. It proposes to add 2 more scheduled sittings of 6 hours that would fully function.
(a) What was the Assembly's productivity?
(b) How many hours would it have needed to function to reach 78 per cent of the 120?
(c) By how many hours did it fall short of that?
(d) Will adding 2 fully functioning sittings of 6 hours be enough to reach 78 per cent of the new schedule? Decide with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 78/120 x 100 = 65 per cent. (b) 0.78 x 120 = 93.6 hours. (c) 93.6 - 78 = 15.6 hours. (d) New schedule 132 hours; 78 + 12 = 90 hours functioned; 90/132 = 68.2 per cent, below 78 per cent. So it is not enough.
s: Computes 65 per cent
Computes 93.6 hours
Computes a shortfall of 15.6 hours
Computes 68.2 per cent for the new plan and says it is not enough
